name: Taman Negara National Park
blurb: Ancient lowland rainforest: figs, hornbills, tapir, gaur and the Malayan tiger.

tip.title: Remove the fig trees
tip.text: Figs feed hornbills, macaques and leaf monkeys. Set Fig trees to -100% and watch the fruit-eaters drop.

notes: The story and why it matters come from the Wikipedia articles listed below (Taman Negara, Malayan tiger, Malayan tapir). Individual species and links have not been checked one by one. Feeding links that match a GloBI (Global Biotic Interactions) record are marked in the node details, with a link to the records. A few links were added from GloBI records.

nodes.desc: Only a small fraction of light reaches the dim forest floor, so canopy trees capture most of the energy that enters the web.
Break down fallen wood, leaves and carcasses, returning nutrients to the soil.
Figs fruit heavily and are an important food for many forest birds and mammals.
Largest land animal of the reserve; a wide-ranging browser and grazer that opens paths and moves through the forest.
Small forest deer that eats leaves, fruit and shoots; prey of tigers and other large predators.
Omnivorous monkey that eats fruit, seeds and small animals.
Large forest bird whose diet is dominated by fruit, including figs, plus some insects and small animals.
Big lizard near streams that hunts amphibians and also feeds on carrion.

nodes.name: Malayan tiger
nodes.desc: Top predator of the reserve; it takes large hoofed prey, including barking deer (muntjac) and wild cattle such as gaur.

story: Taman Negara in Peninsular Malaysia covers 4,343 km² and is estimated to be more than 130 million years old. It was established in 1938 and 1939 as King George V National Park. Mount Tahan, at 2,187 m, is the peninsula's highest point.
matters: It is an important conservation area for endangered Malayan tigers and Asian elephants. It lies on the traditional lands of Orang Asli groups such as the Batek, whose use rights are recognised in law.
